name: Cannula filler technique

lead: A cannula is a blunt, flexible tube used to place dermal filler under the skin in place of a sharp needle. It is used for areas such as nasolabial folds and the midface.
Published evidence specific to the cannula is thin: a few registered trials of individual products, without a broad comparison of safety against needles.

paras: Filler is pushed through a rounded-tip tube inserted at one entry point and advanced through tissue, depositing product along the path.
Filler risks include bruising, swelling, infection, allergic reactions and, rarely, vascular embolization with vision loss or skin necrosis [1]. Fillers are regulated as medical devices.

lead: The cannula filler technique is a method of placing injectable dermal filler through a blunt-tipped, flexible tube (a cannula) rather than a sharp needle. Practitioners typically make a single entry point in the skin and thread the cannula through the tissue to deposit product over a wider area. Fillers themselves are substances injected into skin or deeper tissue to smooth lines or add volume, and hyaluronic acid is the most common type [1].

Published human research on cannula delivery is limited to registered trials of specific products and devices. One completed phase 2 trial registered a metallic cannula against a standard needle for nasolabial fold augmentation [2], and a post-market study registered a hyaluronic acid product delivered by cannula for the same area [3]. Fillers are regulated as medical devices in the US and, with a CE mark, in the UK and European Economic Area [1].

paras: In the cannula approach, filler is delivered through a tube with a rounded tip, which is inserted through a small skin opening and advanced along tissue planes. The alternative is a sharp needle used to inject at multiple points. Wikipedia's general article on dermal fillers does not discuss needles or cannulas specifically [1], so descriptions of the technique come mainly from clinical trial registrations and practitioner accounts.

Dermal fillers in general are associated with bruising, redness, pain and itching, with infection and allergic reactions less common [1]. Rare but serious events include embolization of filler into arteries supplying the eye, which can cause vision loss that is usually permanent, and delayed skin necrosis [1]. Which of these risks differ between cannulas and needles has been a subject of practitioner debate; the sources available here do not report comparative rates, and proponents of each tool disagree.

Registered studies include a phase 2 trial comparing a metallic cannula with a standard needle for nasolabial fold augmentation in 25 participants, started in 2009 and listed as completed [2]. A 50-person trial of a hyaluronic acid filler (RHA) placed with a cannula in nasolabial folds began in 2021 and is listed as completed [3], and a 60-person study of a bridging technique for nasolabial folds began recruiting in late 2025 [4]. Registrations alone do not report outcomes, and no published synthesis comparing cannula and needle safety is cited here.
